projects.name: HR Matching Data Platform

projects.name: Verdaca / Praxis

projects.name: AI Adoption Measurement Framework
projects.one_line: Method and scripts for measuring whether AI coding agents speed up delivery: merged-change unit, cost allocation from fixed subscriptions, counter-metrics.

projects.name: Seismic Facies Classification Pipeline
projects.one_line: MLOps pipeline rebuilt on the public F3 benchmark: one scikit-learn pipeline, leak-free evaluation, MLflow promotion gate and CI that can fail.

projects.name: AI Coaching Platform Rebuild: Release Hardening & Human-Coaching Integration
projects.one_line: Team rebuild of an AI coaching assistant. Andrey owned release hardening, merge-safety gates and the integration of human coaches from a partner platform.

projects.name: MCP Server Spike & Decision Memo
projects.one_line: One-day spike plus decision memo on exposing AI coaching through MCP: a small TypeScript server, stateless design, GDPR scope line and auth plan.

projects.name: LangGraph AI Concierge
projects.one_line: Travel concierge on a LangGraph StateGraph with rules-then-LLM routing, a 40-query routing eval comparing Haiku and Opus, and an offline test suite.

projects.name: Context Engineering Template

projects.name: Swiss Electricity Price Forecasting — MSc Thesis
projects.one_line: MSc thesis forecasting hourly Swiss day-ahead electricity prices with OLS, Ridge, Lasso, ARX and neural networks, plus forecast combination. Graded 5/6.

projects.name: Interview foundations (general topics, not a project)
projects.one_line: General interview topics, not a project: LLM evaluation, RAG, LLM system design, FINMA and Swiss regulation with model risk, and Python fundamentals.

projects.name: flutter_agent_harness (open-source study, not Andrey's project)
projects.one_line: Study notes on someone else's open-source Dart agent harness (loop, providers, compaction, approvals, subagents, quality gates, AI-run delivery). Andrey read it and did not build it.

projects.name: AI certification review (study course, not a project)
projects.one_line: Andrey's review of his AI certification practice questions (AWS, Databricks, Claude agent development), reorganised by topic with the 2026 view: fundamentals, tool design, agent control, context, structured output, retrieval, production, safety.

projects.name: Deep agents and multi-agent systems (study course, not a project)
projects.one_line: Andrey's plain-English study course on deep agents and multi-agent systems with Azure as the base: when a team beats one agent, orchestration patterns, hand-overs, A2A, APM, Python memory and data types, Dart vs Python vs Rust, safety and evaluation.

projects.name: Knowledge graphs and LLM wikis (study course and review of my own systems, not a project)
projects.one_line: Andrey's plain-English study course on knowledge graphs, GraphRAG, LLM wikis and retrieval in 2026, plus an honest review of his own code graphs, wikis, catalogue and digest archive, with a gap analysis.

notes.summary: How the matching system works end to end: rule-based dbt filters cut about 78M candidate-position pairs to about 2M, then a multi-task neural ranker scores them. Batch nightly plus an online path with a training/serving skew risk.
questions: How does the HR matching system work end to end?
Why filter first and rank second?
What is the training/serving skew risk in your ranking system?

notes.summary: How the SQL data layer was restructured: about 650 dbt models on BigQuery, shared macros removing about 900 duplicated lines, tests from none to about 148. Incremental MERGE cut bytes scanned 94% on one model but not on the other.
questions: How did you use dbt and BigQuery in the matching platform?
How did you cut BigQuery query cost?
When does an incremental dbt model not help?

notes.summary: How I proved a large SQL refactor changed nothing: compile-diff, exhaustive checks of three functions, row-level parity on three final tables and an outcome check, while live sources drifted about 4 rows a minute.
questions: How did you prove the SQL refactor did not change the results?
How do you test a data pipeline when the sources keep changing?
What can a parity test not prove?

notes.summary: Three business rules (skill, seniority, location) added as guarded SQL filters so pairs the staffing desk would reject are never scored. Covers NULL-safe logic, fail-open defaults and sizing by simulation because no live rows existed.
questions: How did you handle NULLs in the business rules?
Fail-open or fail-closed for the matching rules, and why?
How did you validate the rules when there was no live data?

notes.summary: How I tested whether a hand-built location-fit feature could be retired: permutation importance, retraining without it, segment checks and Integrated Gradients. The retrain decided it: effect -0.0012 NDCG, below the 0.002 threshold.
questions: How do you decide whether a feature can be removed from a model?
What is permutation importance and what are its pitfalls?
How did you separate statistical from practical significance?

notes.summary: A candid review of what I'd change on the matching project: dbt unit tests, model contracts, pinned-input data diffs, cost caps and small merges. Budget estimates were off by 12x and 36x; four linked changes were still unmerged at departure.
questions: What would you do differently on the HR matching project?
What went wrong with the cost estimates there?
Why are small merges better than one joint merge?

notes.summary: How the governed AI workflow is structured: ports (Protocols and frozen DTOs), Mem0 and Letta adapters, a composition root and contract tests run against each adapter. Key rule: the LLM port returns tokens, never dollars.
questions: How is the governed AI workflow architected?
How do you avoid vendor lock-in for the memory store and model provider?
What are contract tests per adapter?

notes.summary: The auth-first gateway: OIDC token verification with JWKS keys, nonce replay protection, per-user budgets and an allow-list, all before any model call. Explains the spend-blind bug: the budget gate read a meter that never saw real spend.
questions: How does the workflow authenticate users?
What was the spend-blind bug?
How do you prevent replay attacks with JWTs?

notes.summary: How model cost is computed and recorded: LiteLLM calls, a per-million-token price table, Decimal arithmetic, stop reasons and truncation flags. A recorded run of four calls cost about $0.03; the reviewer calls were about 80% of spend.
questions: How much does one governed-workflow run cost?
How do you track LLM cost per call?
What happens when a model output is truncated?

notes.summary: The core mechanism: producer, blind reviewer and synthesizer in four model calls, one backtrack, typed outcomes (answer, clarify, abstain, escalate) and a JSON receipt with a SHA-256 content hash. The hash is explicitly not a signature.
questions: How does the deliberation loop work?
What is in a receipt and can it be tampered with?
Is a hash the same as a signature?

notes.summary: How the workflow was exposed to Claude Desktop through an MCP server: FastMCP, six tools, stdio transport, logs redirected to a file. Called once end to end from Desktop (27 s, about $0.03); this path has no per-user auth.
questions: How did the workflow connect to Claude Desktop?
What is the stdio transport in MCP?
How strong is the evidence that the MCP integration works?

notes.summary: How testing and CI were audited: a false green (tests untracked, CI scoped to a sub-folder) exposed by a fresh clone with 36 failures, then fixed. Covers 1,453 CI kernel tests, AST gates and the no_waiver pin, and what green does not prove.
questions: How is the governed AI workflow tested?
What was the false green incident?
What does a passing test suite not prove?

notes.summary: Honest retrospective: eight weeks of ports, gates and auth before the core ran once; the first real deliberation then needed only about 1,000 lines. Lists limits found (hedge-dropping, self-critique) and what to build first today.
questions: What would you do differently on Verdaca?
What limits did you find in the deliberation output?
Why did the core run so late in the project?

notes.summary: Why 'AI made us faster' needs evidence: METR found developers believed they were 20% faster but were 19% slower, and DORA frames AI as an amplifier. Argues for a tiered metric set pairing every speed metric with a quality counter-metric.
questions: How do you measure whether AI coding tools make a team faster?
Why is developer sentiment not evidence?
What are counter-metrics and why pair them with speed metrics?

notes.summary: Defines the unit of delivery as a ticket with a merged pull request; on a first sample the Done column overstated delivery by about 20%. Covers the PR lifecycle, vote-proxy review timing and reporting distributions, not per-PR averages.
questions: What counts as delivered work in the AI measurement framework?
Why is a closed ticket not the same as delivery?
How do you measure pull request review wait?

notes.summary: How a fixed monthly AI tool subscription is allocated to tickets by cache-read token share, reported as median, quartiles and p90 with an explicit unattributed share. Allocated plus unattributed equals the bill; delivered tickets spanned about 170x.
questions: How do you allocate a fixed AI subscription cost to tickets?
What does one delivered ticket cost in AI spend?
Why report cost distributions instead of an average?

notes.summary: The token-counting bugs found before publishing any cost: Claude totals about 2x too high (usage repeated per content block) and Codex too low (counter resets on resume). Fixes, hashed frozen snapshots, an independent audit script and a public retraction.
questions: What bugs did you find in the token counts?
How did you validate the numbers before publishing?
How do you handle a published figure that turns out to be wrong?

notes.summary: Cost dissection of one outlier ticket: 89% of token volume came from one never-reset parent conversation; 13 subagents were only about 11%. Late turns cost about 8x early ones; fixes are phase resets, batching and disk artifacts.
questions: Why do long AI coding sessions get expensive?
How much do subagents contribute to AI coding cost?
How can you cut AI coding token spend?

notes.summary: The tooling: standard-library-only Python collectors for Claude and Codex logs, pull-request APIs and step events, with sanitised outputs, hashed snapshots and 160+ tests. Specifies a nine-field step-event contract; step attribution is mostly unbuilt.
questions: What scripts did you build for AI adoption measurement?
How did you protect privacy in the metrics?
What would you add next for step attribution?

notes.summary: Post-mortem of the first pipeline: labels were random numbers, so every metric sat at chance (accuracy 0.49 against 0.52 for always-majority). The drift check compared two halves of one sample and could not fail. Explains noise versus leakage.
questions: Why did the first seismic pipeline fail?
How do you tell label noise from data leakage?
Why does a baseline matter when reporting a model score?

notes.summary: The rebuild's data and task: the public F3 North Sea facies benchmark, 32x32 patches labelled at the centre pixel. Test accuracy 0.717 but macro-F1 0.514; classes 4 and 5 are almost never found (recall 0.09 and 0.02).
questions: What dataset and task does the seismic project use?
What accuracy does the seismic model reach?
Which facies classes does the model miss and why?

notes.summary: Training to serving as one artefact: a scikit-learn pipeline (scaler, PCA 32, gradient boosting) logged to MLflow and loaded unchanged by the API, so served predictions equal trained ones. Uses skops instead of pickle.
questions: How is the seismic model served?
How do you avoid training/serving skew?
Why use skops instead of pickle?

notes.summary: How evaluation was made leak-free: contiguous section blocks with a 10-section gap, validation separate from the benchmark's test volume, the promotion gate reading validation only, and test1 scored once per run.
questions: How did you prevent data leakage in the seismic project?
Why not split patches randomly?
How do you keep a test set honest?

notes.summary: The promotion gate and registry: a new model becomes champion only if it beats the majority baseline on accuracy and macro-F1 and the incumbent on macro-F1; ties lose. Uses MLflow aliases; rejected versions stay registered for audit.
questions: How does a model get promoted to production in the seismic pipeline?
What is champion/challenger in MLflow?
How would you compare two classifiers fairly?

notes.summary: CI that can actually fail: make ci runs 27 tests plus a train, gate and serve demo on a committed fixture. Lists what is not built (drift monitoring, retraining, Docker) and what a real monitor needs (PSI, reference window).
questions: Is the seismic project's CI meaningful?
What monitoring and drift detection exists in the seismic pipeline?
What is missing from the pipeline and what would you add?

notes.summary: The architecture of the coaching platform Andrey joined: Azure Functions v4 code on Container Apps, SPA and API on one origin behind nginx, Slack as a separate app, a provider switch with no silent fallback, and Sonnet-for-chat, Haiku-for-generation tiering.
questions: How is the AI coaching platform architected?
How is the Claude model chosen per task on the coaching platform?
Why is there no automatic fallback between Claude providers?

notes.summary: Release-readiness controls: a two-flag kill switch at the single model-call chokepoint, cross-organisation isolation tests with sentinels, an encryption-coverage census gate and post-deploy smoke tests with timer liveness. Written after all timers had silently been dead.
questions: How did you make the coaching platform safe to release?
How do you test tenant data isolation?
How does your kill switch work?

notes.summary: Merge safety for a team landing about five AI-written PRs a day: a silent-revert guard using git blame and ancestry, and wiring 575 frontend tests that never ran into CI. Both gates were proven able to fail and fail closed.
questions: How do you stop AI-written PRs from silently deleting merged work?
How does the silent-revert guard work?
How did you find tests that existed but never ran?

notes.summary: Andrey's main slice: integrating human coaches from a separate partner platform via OAuth client credentials, a capability enable-list, service-aware error mapping and partner-first booking with a journal. His fix: cancel used the wrong id, so slots stayed blocked.
questions: What did you personally build on the coaching platform?
What was the cancel-booking bug and how did you fix it?
How do you integrate with a system you do not control?

notes.summary: Andrey's personal AI delivery method: read-only routing of each ticket to one of seven process levels, separate contexts per phase, disposable clones, a code graph with a freshness check and a gated wiki. The effect is admitted to be unmeasured.
keywords: how do you work with ai agents
questions: How do you work with AI coding agents day to day?

notes.summary: MCP basics and how the spike works: JSON-RPC, tools versus resources versus prompts, stdio and Streamable HTTP, Zod schemas with structuredContent, and a stub coaching backend with two tools. Notes that the booking tool is not idempotent.
questions: What is MCP and how does it work?
What is the difference between tools, resources and prompts in MCP?

notes.summary: Why the MCP server keeps no state: a new server per request so any serverless instance can answer, versus sessions that need affinity (1/N chance of reaching the owner). Covers the July 2026 spec dropping sessions and the handle pattern.
questions: Why is the MCP server stateless?
How do you keep multi-turn state on a stateless protocol?
What changed in the July 2026 MCP specification?

notes.summary: What to expose through third-party AI platforms before identity and a DPIA exist: reference data, single-turn advice and booking now; memory, progress and multi-turn deferred. Covers GDPR basics, prompt injection and a five-question scope-line test.

What is a DPIA and when is it needed?

notes.summary: What auth an MCP server needs today: act as an OAuth 2.1 resource server with Protected Resource Metadata, PKCE, audience-bound tokens, per-tool scopes and a client registration choice. The spike has no auth; the memo's API-key-first advice is critiqued.
questions: How should an MCP server be authenticated?
What is PKCE and why is it required?
Why is token passthrough forbidden in MCP?

notes.summary: How the concierge works: a seven-node LangGraph StateGraph with two conditional edges and TypedDict state, and the sticky-route bug where turn 2 reused turn 1's route and no answer was printed. The fix resets 13 turn-scoped fields each turn.
questions: How does the LangGraph concierge work?
What was the per-turn reset bug?
Is the concierge really multi-agent?

notes.summary: Rules-then-LLM routing: regex rules decide clear cases free (threshold 0.72); otherwise one Haiku call must return a route with confidence of at least 0.75, else fall back to a clarifying question or human hand-off. A model call cost $0.00041 on Haiku versus $0.00134 on Opus.
questions: How does the router decide between rules and the LLM?
What does one routing decision cost?
What happens when the model is not confident?

notes.summary: The routing evaluation: 40 labelled queries, three arms. Rules only 52.5%, with Opus 62.5%, with Haiku 65.0%; the 2.5-point gap is one row, not a result, and the whole LLM gain is 4-5 rag rows. Covers sample size and intervals.
questions: How accurate is the concierge router?
Is Haiku as good as Opus for routing?
How would you design a routing eval?

notes.summary: How the test suite was made honest: 497 offline tests, but the first version had about 50 wording or layout tests and one test asserting the bug. Adds a three-turn session test, fakes only at the edges and README numbers pinned to data.
questions: How do you test an LLM app without calling the API?
What was wrong with the first concierge test suite?
How do you keep README claims true?

notes.summary: How the template works: a stateless dispatcher in CLAUDE.md, state in files, the write/select/compress/isolate moves and sized pipelines (Micro to Large). The full pipeline used 613,670 tokens on a small task versus an estimated under 100k for one prompt.
questions: What is context engineering?
How does the Claude Code template work?
Did the full agent pipeline pay off on a small task?

notes.summary: The seven subagents and their privileges: per-role tool allowlists (reviewers are read-only), a blind reviewer that sees only the diff, a 9-cell conflict matrix, size tiers and circuit breakers. A missing tool is a control; prompt rules are only requests.
questions: How are subagents set up and restricted?
What is a blind reviewer?

notes.summary: Hooks that actually block: the first version could never fire (wrong config shape, env vars instead of stdin JSON, exit 1 instead of 2). The fix has a red-then-green record (5 pass, 26 fail, then 31/31) and a live session where a write was blocked.
questions: How do Claude Code hooks block an action?
How did you verify the hooks really work?
Why did the first hooks never fire?

notes.summary: The thesis setup: forecasting Swiss hourly day-ahead prices from 26,304 rows, with cleaning, lag features, an ADF stationarity test (-8.39), a chronological 70/30 split and HAC errors. Defines the day-ahead information set that same-day features violate.
questions: What problem does the electricity price thesis solve?
What is stationarity and how did you test it?
What data and features were used?

notes.summary: The model ladder: OLS, Ridge, Lasso, ARX and a tuned MLP. Test MSE ran from 57.4 (tuned network) and 59.3 (Lasso) to 83.8 for ARX; gaps among the top models are smaller than the network's run-to-run spread.
questions: Which models did you compare in the thesis?
Did the neural network beat the linear models?
What were the test errors of each model?

notes.summary: Forecast combination with equal, R2-weighted and constrained least squares weights. In-sample CLS scored MSE 55.4 against 57.4 for equal weights, but on 2024 the simple average beat every single model, illustrating the combination puzzle.
questions: Why did the simple average win in the thesis?
Does combining forecasts help?
What is the forecast combination puzzle?

notes.summary: The bugs Andrey found in his own thesis code: same-day maximum and production leakage (+14% MSE when fixed), combination weights fitted on the test period, the dummy-variable trap and misleading MAPE. The repository is kept frozen as submitted.
questions: What mistakes are in your thesis code?
What is the same-day leakage bug?
Why is MAPE a misleading metric here?

notes.summary: How to evaluate an LLM application: golden sets, programmatic scorers before LLM judges, judge biases and calibration against humans, confidence intervals and sample size (97 items for plus or minus 10 points), CI regression suites and FINMA-style tests.

questions: How do you evaluate an LLM application?

questions: Explain RAG and how you would build one for a bank.

questions: How would you design an LLM system for a bank?
